text: We can move the deletion of existing Pods to a dedicated controller (or even to ). However, workload controllers still must obey the rule: when has , stop Pod creation and wait until is gone. If the controller that creates Pods does not pause while victim Pods terminate, it immediately creates replacement Pods. Then the controller and the workload controller fight each other in a loop (one creates Pods while the other deletes them). This loop also keeps the finalizer on and blocks deletion. A dedicated controller reduces the responsibility of workload controllers, but it does not remove the fragile contract around pausing Pod creation and controller delegation.

text: Thanks for looking! Nobody starts the interactive REPL on purpose with stdin set to NUL. The trouble is that tools which run commands non-interactively hand the process NUL as stdin, and since NUL is a character device, reports True. So an accidental bare , or with an empty heredoc, lands in pyrepl instead of reading EOF and exiting. Where I hit it: AI coding agents. Claude Code's shell tool on Windows runs every command with stdin = NUL and output captured, so anyone using it on Windows can hit this. The process never returns: it spins writing tracebacks (about 4 MB in 3 seconds here) until the tool's timeout kills it. hyperfine also defaults stdin to NUL (that's how #133430 got there), and CI runners and schedulers commonly do the same. The basic REPL ( ) reads EOF and exits at once, which is what these tools need. A possible check: fails on NUL even though succeeds: So pyrepl could fall back to the basic REPL when fails on stdin, or at least stop retrying after the first from .

text: **Update / root cause on my side (follow-up to my earlier comments):** In my case this turned out **not** to be a bug in the integration or in – the entity had been **disabled in the entity registry**. A disabled entity is never added to hass, so it never subscribes to the dispatcher signal and therefore never fires . After re-enabling the entity and restarting Home Assistant, everything works again on 2026.10.1. To verify, I ran a copy of the core integration (unchanged apart from added log lines) as a custom component and traced the full path. Before the fix: …and nothing else – no entity was listening. After re-enabling the entity: **Important for others landing here:** the debug line is **not** the cause of missing events. The integration uses the library's raw ERP1 callback ( ), which is emitted *before* EEP decoding. text: One reservation I have from the build backend side of things is that it's not fully clear to me how to wire this up while at the same time allowing users to choose. My understanding from the PEP is that this is "just" about ensuring that globally distributed binaries (Linux distro packages, conda, cibuildwheel outputs published to PyPI, etc.) don't hinder adoption for users that need to do tracing. text: Thanks @user. [PEP 831](http enables frame pointers by default in CPython and strongly recommends the same throughout Python's native ecosystem, including extensions and their dependencies. The recommendation also covers local builds. Each build system and project needs to work out how to implement it across its builds; the PEP cannot prescribe that for every setup. We expect this to take time, and that's fine. The goal remains frame pointers throughout the native ecosystem. Your static-library example is a real limitation. The setting needs to reach those libraries and subprojects when they are compiled, since adding flags only to the bindings leaves gaps in stack unwinding. Dependencies supplied as binaries would need to be rebuilt by whoever distributes them. There are examples to follow. [Ubuntu](http and [Fedora](http already adopted frame-pointer defaults. Ubuntu originally exempted Python; upstream CPython 3.15 now enables them. [python-build-standalone's change](http adds them to shared target flags, which dependency builds such as [SQLite](http also consume. Ideally, manylinux and other dependency-build pipelines would apply this to the libraries they build too. That will require coordination and rebuilding over time. For Meson, would a build-wide setting that reaches subprojects be workable? This PR is intended to make the relevant information available to backends, while projects work through how to apply it to their dependencies.

text: I have reproduced a hang in both and on an M1 Mac by dropping a single client UDP datagram in a temporary diagnostic build. Both get stuck in . Sampling the process showed it waiting in through the blocking QUIC read path. The client is explicitly nonblocking, while the accepted server connection inherits blocking mode from the listener. I checked this at runtime: returned 0 for the client and 1 for the server. The underlying UDP sockets are nonblocking in both cases. In these two scripts, the same interpreter thread drives both endpoints and advances the simulated clock. A blocking continues to service the server's QUIC events, but the interpreter can't run the client to retransmit the lost data. The simulated clock also stops advancing. The interpreter own 60 second deadline can't interrupt that call. Making the accepted server connection nonblocking lets both scripts recover from the dropped datagram and finish. All 114 RADIX scripts also passed with that experimental change. To check whether this was hiding a problem in blocking reads, I kept the server blocking and added a temporary worker to tick the client and advance the simulated clock during the read. Both scripts recovered and completed with still returning 1 for the server. Ticking the client alone still hung, as did advancing the clock alone. This points to a RADIX execution problem. RADIX deliberately enables for its blocking tests, including . We should keep that support and make blocking mode an explicit choice for tests that provide independent progress. I will work on a PR for this.

text: Quick update here. We've been working on figuring out the cause of the task failures and have made some progress in the past few months. The RAM itself should be fine, as it passed every single test. Since the SIGILL issue can be observed on both builders (mipsle and mips64le) and even in kernel space (see http we decided to dive into it first. We deployed a BadInstr (a register in CP0) check in the reserved instruction (RI) exception handler, and found it somehow mismatched the instruction read from RAM every time we saw a task failure caused by SIGILL. In this failure pattern, the decoder sees an illegal instruction and traps into an RI exception, with BadInstr containing what it has seen. The instruction located in RAM is still legal. This hints that the instruction cache and the data cache behave differently in some edge cases! The illegal instruction in BadInstr, however, is never similar to the legal one in RAM. We haven't seen any cache error either (all cache levels have internal ECC). Thus, it's not a bitflip issue. Next, we deployed a hack to the BadInstr check to verify our theory. The hack flushes the instruction cache by calling and returns to userspace to resume execution. Guess what, the execution finishes without trapping into another RI exception. Task failures caused by SIGILL are gone since then! So it seems SIGSEGV is just another failure pattern where the mismatched instruction in the instruction cache happens to be legal. The same failure pattern also has the potential to cause other categories of test failures. Currently, we are still working on figuring out the root cause and hopefully fixing or working around it. We suspect a kernel bug (faulty context switch?) or an undiscovered CPU errata.

text: I need to correct my own analysis in the issue description — it was wrong, and I apologise for the noise. UnicodeEncodeError.start / .end are indices into exc.object, which for BufferedIncrementalEncoder is the concatenation self.buffer + input (the str that _buffer_encode receives), not a byte offset. For the reproducer: enc = codecs.getincrementalencoder("idna")() enc.encode("é") # held in the buffer enc.encode("." + "a"*64, True) exc.object is "é." + "a"*64 (66 characters). "a"*64 starts at index 2 of that string, so start=2, end=66 is correct. I confused the byte length of the punycode-encoded label (b"xn--9ca", 7 bytes) with the character length of the label inside exc.object ("é", 1 character). len(encoded) is not comparable to the str index that start/end refer to. The existing code (size += len(label)) is correct. My suggested change (size += len(encoded)) would produce start=8, end=72, which is wrong: end=72 exceeds len(exc.object)=66. So there is no bug in Lib/encodings/idna.py. I'm closing this issue as not-a-bug. @user — sorry for sending you down this path. The PR #159233 should be closed; there is nothing to fix here. text: I have opened #33213. The packet loss filter from my earlier probe isn't needed to trigger the hang. After a key update, OpenSSL retains the previous receive keys for one probe timeout (PTO). If the client starts another update while the server still retains those keys, the server discards its packets, as allowed by [RFC 9001 section 6.5](http The peers can have very different PTOs. RADIX advances its fake clock by 1 ms per interpreter step, so extra handshake retries can inflate the initial RTT estimate. During the data loop, the server's estimate can stay high while the client gets shorter samples. The client waits three of its own PTOs after confirmation of the previous update, but the server can still be retaining its old keys when the next update arrives. The blocking server read then stops the interpreter, which also needs to drive the client's retransmission. It can't advance the fake clock while it's inside either, so recovery gets stuck. The two SIGABRT jobs look like the same hang. At their source revisions, the scripts following the last completed iterations are these same key update tests, and the elapsed time matches the watchdog calling after 1800 seconds. The PR makes clients and listeners nonblocking when RADIX creates them, and accepted connections inherit that setting. Waiting reads can return control to the interpreter, while stays enabled for tests that need blocking . The regression delays an ACK to give the server a larger PTO, then exercises successive client key updates. The old setup hangs with the mode checks removed; with the fix, it recovers without a packet loss filter. I have checked the full RADIX suite on my M1 with threads and without them, keeping the usual skips in the latter build. The new test also passed 150 repetitions, with qlog enabled for half of those runs.

text: One of the issues is, that we would like to support the eviction of a PodGroup and the deallocation of resources (e.g. ResourceClaims) via other mechanisms other than preemption, but also during general eviction (e.g. node drain). While keeping the workload controllers in a loop. So, if we were to introduce preemption specific fields or conditions to implement the pod group pod termination and resource deallocation, we would also have to solve synchronization with other mechanisms later on. This is one of the key features of the eviction request that plans to add PodGroup eviction support in the next release. We have alreadu defined the final state of Eviction of a Pod as a process termination, not necessarily deletion. This means that the Pod can still be present in etcd, and we can observe the status/logs after the eviction is complete. This is different from traditional eviction. Similarly, we have to define the final state for Eviction of a PodGroup. It seems reasonable to base this on a termination of all current pods. This could be controller dependent and new pods could be created in the meantime. I will draft, how the preemption/eviction of a PodGroup could work using an EvictionRequest: To support the resource deallocation, we could introduce an evictionResponders field on the podGroup object (similar to what we that in the Pod API): Which could result in the following Eviction object and status, where the scheduler could inject the preemption behavior Scheduler could simply observe until the workload controller does its own custom gang termination logic. If there is none (e.g. the workload responder is not present), we would jump straight to preemption (default behavior). The main question is how to avoid blocking preemption for too long. What kind of guarantees does the scheduling preemption want to provide to workloads? Is it sufficient to watch the heartbeats, or should we introduce a fallback or some kind of a deadline to prevent resource starvation? Responder priorities also allows scheduling to introduce multiple breakpoints when needed to achieve the desired eviction semantics. As mentioned, the EvicictionRequest also handles the concurrency and multiple Eviction requesters (preemption, node drain, kubelet eviction) can be reconcilled together. This approach could also be used if we wanted to remove the PodGroup object, instead of just terminating the child pods. The integration part is optional for the controllers; it is only necessary if they require custom termination/migration than what default preemption offers.

text: This fixes the KNOWN_BUGS entry "telnet code does not handle partial writes properly". Only send_telnet_data() loops on short writes. The option negotiation, the NAWS suboption and the TTYPE, XDISPLOC and NEW_ENVIRON suboption replies each go out with one Curl_xfer_send() call, and the number of bytes written is ignored. On a short write the reply is cut off and the server never gets the closing IAC SE. The poll-and-send loop now lives in a send_telnet_raw() helper that every send uses. sendsuboption() also stops at the first failed send instead of ignoring the result of the middle part. Test 1717 is new. negtelnetserver.py now asks the client for NEW-ENVIRON, parses suboptions up to IAC SE and appends the received variables to its echo. It waits until both the data line and the NEW-ENVIRON reply have arrived (with a timeout), so the result does not depend on which one the client sends first. The test sets a NEW_ENV variable and forces partial writes with CURL_DBG_SOCK_WPARTIAL=50. Without the fix it fails every time; with it, it passes, and so do the other TELNET tests (1326, 1327, 1452, 1548, 1714, 3555). checksrc and pythonlint pass. The first CI run showed 1717 failing: the test server echoed the line before the client's NEW-ENVIRON reply arrived. The third commit fixes that race.

text: Can you attach some debug logs? The tracebacks alone aren't really that useful. ZHA will disconnect from a radio only in a few scenarios: - Its internal software watchdog detects that the radio is dead: this means the radio has stopped responding to simple "are you alive?" pings for 30 seconds. - The radio itself reports that it has crashed and rebooted. ZHA will then re-connect to your radio. - The physical connection to the radio has terminated. A USB unplug or a TCP server connection closing, for example. Your SLZB devices have two chips onboard: an ESP32 chip that acts as the TCP server, and a Zigbee chip that ZHA tries to communicate with. If the Zigbee chip crashes/resets, your radio stops functioning even though the ESP32 half still "works". Silicon Labs radios will enter a failure state if ZHA does not acknowledge a message from the radio within ~7 seconds. If you choose to use a networked coordinator, you introduce Ethernet (or WiFi...) instability and latency, the ESP32 proxy, and finally code running on the ESP32 proxy between ZHA and your Zigbee chip. If any part of that chain is unstable, you'll see disconnects. ZHA is unlikely to be the problem here so there isn't much we can do to fix it.

text: Cross-linking a much stronger reproduction of the same signature found while investigating why CPU profile captures were killing a Go TUI app on Linux. **Signature:** process dies with SIGKILL (exit 137) from outside — no panic, no runtime fatal error, nothing in dmesg/journal, no OOM ( zero), no rlimits ( unlimited), no seccomp (mode 0), no cgroup caps — while CPU profiling is enabled. Same as this issue, but deterministic (100% of runs, dies within ~1s of arming) and it reproduces in **plain C with no Go runtime involved**, which is why I am posting it here rather than treating it as a Go bug: **Isolation matrix** (all on the same machine, x86_64, 12-core): | program | outcome | |---|---| | C: + busy loop | killed, exit 137 | | C: same timer on + | survives, 547 ticks delivered | | C: + (no thread targeting) | survives, 544 ticks delivered | | Go: busy loop + at 100Hz | survives | | Go: busy loop + only | killed in under 1s | | Go: busy loop, no profiling | survives | So the lethal combination is specifically a **CPU-time clock with thread-targeted delivery** — exactly what the Go runtime arms per-M since it moved off (#35057 / #65856 context). Linux 7.2 merged a timer-subsystem hardening series (posix-cpu-timers/hrtimer anti-DoS rework by tglx), which is my prime suspect for the behavioral change; regression status vs 6.x is not yet established on this machine. text: Thanks for pointing me to #12155. I understand why importing Windows CA certificates was added: it lets curl complete a chain when a server omits an intermediate certificate, which matters in the enterprise proxy scenario reported there. My concern is specifically about trust, rather than using those certificates for chain building. The Windows CA store supplies intermediate certificates; their presence there alone should not make them trust anchors. Currently they are added to OpenSSL’s trusted X509_STORE, where PARTIAL_CHAIN can allow verification to end at one of them even if its root is not trusted. The ROOT-only change in this PR avoids that trust expansion, but it also loses the missing-intermediate behavior you pointed out. A more complete approach would keep Windows CA certificates available as untrusted chain-building intermediates, while keeping trust anchors separate, along the lines of Chromium’s distinction between issuer lookup and trust. I’m treating this PR as WIP while I investigate whether the more complete approach is practical for curl’s OpenSSL backend.

Without that bond, fails with ATT 0x0e and the motor drops the link. On a local Linux adapter that bond is BlueZ . Released Bleak does not register an , so devices that ask for yes/no confirmation fail with . registers a temporary Agent1 on the Bleak client's D-Bus connection for the duration of . That only exists when the GATT connection is on the Home Assistant host's BlueZ stack. A connection through an ESPHome/Shelly proxy never reaches that D-Bus connection; pairing would have to happen on the proxy's BLE stack. Bleak still has no pairing-callback API for that path ([hbldh/bleak#1864](http still open). @user noted there that ESPHome pairing support is planned once that lands. But unfortunately, Apple's implementation of linker-enabled thread locals [uses pthread keys internally](http which means that by the time our destructor callback is run, the thread local storage might have already been deallocated, thus leaking all our TLS variables. On macOS, the only way to run destructors for linker-enabled TLS variables is to use . text: Here's a first cut at that recommendation, pulling together the priority direction from this thread. No preemption changes involved. Today the tie among same-priority victims is Pod age. Older Pods are treated as more important, and nothing looks at whether the evicted Pod could be rescheduled elsewhere. The practical answer is to use priorities to reflect mobility. - Keep Pods that can be recreated anywhere at lower priorities. They're the ones you'd rather give up. - Pods whose replacement can't schedule anywhere else once evicted (a DaemonSet's generated node affinity, or a nodeSelector matching a single node) should sit above the ones that can move, so they don't get picked as victims. - In multi-tenant clusters this is usually a platform call by whoever manages PriorityClasses, not something each workload owner can do. The one case this doesn't cover is when both competing Pods already sit at the same, highest priority. No configuration can tell them apart there. If this looks right, should this go somewhere in the docs, or is it fine here? AI disclosure: I used an AI assistant to help draft this response.

text: Ok, let's go with RegistrationOptions.Conditional, thank you for the pointers @user. The mediation is specified by the application, not by the options we generate, and I don't want to trust the developer with not omitting mediation by mistake on RegistrationOptions.Conditional registration options, like: However, we can double-check that. Since 1. We agreed that conditional registration is not vulnerable to PIN-setup attacks. ("If it's ever supported, it will almost certainly require setting up a PIN on a security key beforehand.") 2. If UV=1 at registration, the credential is not vulnerable to PIN-setup attacks. 3. If the registration is _not_ conditional, we always have UP=1. (WebAuthn §6.3.2: requireUserPresence is "the constant Boolean value true, or FALSE when options.mediation is set to conditional"; CTAP's authenticatorMakeCredential always performs user presence.) it follows that we only need to reject UV=0 UP=1 in Register, without looking at BE. If our non-conditional options set userVerification required, UV=0 UP=1 can only be from conditional registrations, and the [help-test-crypto-passkey.exe.xyz](http has no such recordings, only 25x UP=0 UV=0 and 42x UP=1 UV=1. In terms of UX this will require UV at registration for some authenticators that don't need it, which will be a bit inconvenient, but it might also fix PIN-capable-without-PIN security keys on Safari and Firefox. The one risk is that an authenticator could someday start doing conditional registrations with UV=0 UP=1 and we'll reject those. Maybe by then we'll have a WebAuthn extension to communicate "UV was not collected but it's set up, relax", who knows. If nothing else, this will make us look less "weird." P.S. it'd be nice if WebAuthn L3 §7.1 initialized uvInitialized to true when UV=1 _or_ UP=0. UP=0 implies conditional creation, which the client only allows right after it mediated an authentication for that origin, so the "additional authentication factor" that §7.2 demands before trusting UV has already been provided, just before the credential. Read as-is, the spec suggests a freshly conditionally-registered credential can't be used for password-less authentication until it goes through a password login, which kinda defeats the point of conditional registration.

text: I searched thoroughly in the recent past and found no existing issue. When I previously raised the issue it was eventually closed without any apparent awareness that there really is a logic bug. The current database query uses ascending order, meaning that it will select the oldest history records. When reloading history to start a session, the query should be selecting the most recent history records -- this requires the query to use descending order. Thus on startup the statistics that use history (e.g., mean) return results based on the oldest history. That incorrect history is used until is eventually replaced by recent history. Thus the bug is visible only at system restart and it fairly quickly disappears. I see no reason why it should not be fixed -- it requires only 3 simple changes in the code.

text: In the energy distribution card, the battery's ↓ arrow is energy charged *into* the battery and ↑ is energy discharged *from* it. So your screenshot shows 4.3 kWh charged and 0 kWh discharged, not 4.3 kWh drawn from the battery. With that, the balance is: 2.93 (grid) + 0.81 (solar) + 0 (from battery) − 0.82 (returned to grid) − 4.3 (into battery) = −1.38 kWh. A negative home consumption is shown as 0 kWh. The battery can't have charged 4.3 kWh when only 3.74 kWh came in, so one of the sensors is assigned the wrong way. In the energy config you posted, the battery has (energy *out of* the battery) set to and (energy *into* the battery) set to . So the 4.3 kWh come from . If the battery was actually discharging, as you wrote, these two are swapped. Swap them in the energy settings ("Energy charged into the battery" / "Energy discharged from the battery"). Zigbee2MQTT has its own device converters, so a device working there doesn't mean ZHA already supports it. Quirks are maintained in [zigpy/zha-device-handlers](http Please open a "Device support request" there for each device (one issue per device, also for devices where only some functions are missing). text: Adding token-level evidence for this issue. I believe this is the root cause rather than a separate bug: the stored OAuth access token is byte-for-byte unchanged across an expiry, which turns the timing inference in the thread above into a direct measurement. **Home Assistant Core:** 2026.10.1 · **OS:** Home Assistant OS 18.3 · **Auth:** (Nabu Casa account linking), not a Personal Access Token. --- ## Summary The SmartThings OAuth access token is issued with (24 h). It is validated and refreshed when the config entry is set up, and then **never refreshed again while the integration runs**. At the credential simply goes stale in place. Home Assistant raises **no reauth flow** and creates **no repair issue**, and the config entry stays , so there is no visible prompt and the integration never recovers on its own. Reloading the config entry refreshes the token in about half a second, which proves the refresh token and the cloud credentials are both valid. What is missing is anything that triggers a refresh during normal operation. --- ## Why nothing refreshes it , : - — . This is the **only** unconditional validation, and it runs once, at setup. - — a coroutine is defined and assigned to , so pysmartthings *is* given a way to refresh. - — the integration then starts one long-lived SSE subscription as a background task ( ). In steady state that subscription makes no request that would call , so the capability is wired up but never exercised. The connection itself stays healthy — #176244 reports keepalives continuing every ~60 s while device events stop — because it is the SmartThings *server* that stops delivering on a subscription whose token has expired. Nothing client-side errors, so nothing triggers reauth. : This has a consequence worth stating explicitly, because it defeats the obvious workaround: **reloading the entry on a schedule does not renew a token that is still valid.** A reload only refreshes inside the last 20 seconds of the token's life. A twice-daily reload therefore bounds the outage at ~12 h; it cannot prevent one. --- ## Evidence ### The stored token does not move From , same entry, 24 h apart. Only a **manual reload** changed it; the automatic path never did. | when | | access token (last 6) | what happened | |---|---|---|---| | 2026-10-12 09:34 (before) | — **6 h in the past** | | failing continuously | | 2026-10-12 09:34 (after a manual entry reload) | | | **refreshed in ~1 s** | | 2026-10-13 09:40 (24 h later, no reload) | — **5 min in the past** | — *unchanged* | failing again | The access token on day two is byte-for-byte the one the reload produced on day one. No refresh was ever attempted in between. ### A reload refreshes it in 0.531 s Measured on 2026-10-14 from the recorder's event and the resulting stored token: ( is set to the moment the token response is processed, so this is the whole reload-and-refresh round trip.) ### Failures resume within minutes of expiry, at a steady rate Token expired . First errors: Measured cadence during the 2026-10-14 outage: two consumers polling every 30 s, i.e. **6 lines a minute, ~8,600 a day**, indefinitely. On this installation it was the single largest source of log volume for weeks before the cause was identified. ### No reauth, no repair issue With the token expired and calls failing: ### Token metadata --- ## What this installation can and cannot show Stated plainly, because an earlier draft of this report overclaimed it. **It cannot show core-side entity degradation.** An earlier version said "every SmartThings call starts failing". That was not demonstrated here and should not be asserted. On this installation only **4 of the core integration's 54 entities are enabled**, all of them switches that change rarely. Across the 2026-10-14 outage (token expired 14:02:58 UTC, reload 15:45:09 UTC) those four logged **zero** state changes — but the 180-minute silence ranks **14th of 103** inter-update gaps in 15 days of recorder history, where normal gaps reach 3+ days. So the silence is unremarkable and proves nothing either way. Nor did any of them go , and logged **nothing at all** across the whole outage. That absence of core-side symptoms is itself the point, and it is what makes the bug so hard to see: the integration that owns the token is not the one making the failing requests. #176244 is the complementary report, from an installation with enough active SmartThings entities for the freeze to be visible. **What it does show** is the token-level fact: the stored credential is never refreshed on the running path, and whatever consumes it fails from onward with no reauth and no repair issue. --- ## Downstream impact on this installation The custom integration ("SamsungTV Smart and Art Mode", TheFab21's fork) is configured , i.e. it reads this entry's stored access token. When the token expires it loses the TV's real HDMI source names and its two light sensors, and logs its own auth failures at the rate above. All 460+ error lines in the 2026-10-14 outage were its, and none were the core integration's. This is noted only to show that the blast radius is wider than the core integration's own entities. The bug is in the core integration. --- ## Workaround in use A scheduled automation reloads the SmartThings config entry twice a day, then the dependent entry shortly after. Per the margin above this is a **recovery** mechanism, not a preventive one: it bounds an outage at ~12 h rather than avoiding it. A second automation reloads the entry 15 s before the stored , i.e. inside the 20-second window where will actually refresh. A sensor ( ) reads out of and a time trigger fires at that value minus 15 s. **Measured on its first live cycle, confirming the mechanism described above:** The 24 h move is the point: an identical reload at any other time of day moves the token by **0 h**, because returns early. That is the cleanest demonstration I can offer that the credential is fine and only the refresh trigger is missing. Note the asymmetry this leaves: the at-expiry reload can only **prevent** a lapse, never recover from one. Once is in the past the trigger has nothing to fire on, which is why the twice-daily reload has to stay as a backstop. Both are workarounds for this bug and should be removable once it is fixed. --- ## What would fix it - Refresh the OAuth token on the running path — e.g. call on a timer derived from , or re-establish the SSE subscription with a fresh token before the old one expires. - Failing that, detect the stalled subscription and raise so Home Assistant starts a reauth flow, instead of leaving the entry and silently stale. PR #182687's periodic REST reconciliation would mask the stall but would keep using the same expired token, so it does not address this.

text: If we take the approach of casting non-string field names to strings, where do we draw the line on acceptable input types for field names? The field names are passed as keys to a dict in the examples in the report, which allows all hashable types, which then includes types like functions, classes and modules, tuples, floats, bools, None - none of which seem to me to translate meaningfully into parameters in an http request. Checking [the docs](http shows that the dict format is one of many supported types for the data parameter - I think the real issue here is that the urlencoded code path is blindly accepting/converting int keys to strings, and the lack of input validation on either the urlencoded code path or the multipart encoded code path then exposes inconsistent behavior. To my mind, the right approach is likely to only accept string-like types in all cases and consistently raise a TypeError rather than depending on the behavior of downstream encoding functions. That would, however, be a breaking change. We already have one example of code that currently "works" and wouldn't anymore if we introduce that change. It also seems likely, given the documented supported input types, that there's a fair bit of complexity involved to do this "correctly". I don't have an authoritative answer, I'd love to hear other opinions on the best course here.

Your camera sends different events in different XML formats (namespaces). pyHik 0.4.7 remembers the format of the first message and expects every later message to use it. text: Docs audit: supply-chain and build gaps (INSTALL, INSTALL-CMAKE, GIT-INFO) Summary Audit of three curl build-related docs (docs/INSTALL.md, docs/INSTALL-CMAKE.md, docs/GIT-INFO.md) found critical gaps in supply-chain verification and CI-ready defaults. For a TLS client with ~10^9 installs, these gaps are not theoretical. Files affected docs/INSTALL.md -- build from source (autotools, CMake, vcpkg) docs/INSTALL-CMAKE.md -- CMake-specific options docs/GIT-INFO.md -- build from git checkout Findings 1. INSTALL.md -- no source verification (critical) No step for SHA256 checksum or GPG signature of downloaded tarballs. User can wget from a mirror and tar xzf without verification. Compromised mirror / MITM / CDN takeover -> backdoored curl. Proposed fix (3 lines before tar xzf): sha256sum -c curl-X.Y.Z.tar.gz.sha256 gpg --verify curl-X.Y.Z.tar.gz.asc curl-X.Y.Z.tar.gz 2. INSTALL-CMAKE.md -- BUILD_TESTING=ON contradicts tests not supported (critical) Doc states tests do not work with CMake, but BUILD_TESTING=ON is the default. ctest runs, fails silently, CI gets false green. Proposed fix: default BUILD_TESTING=OFF until tests are supported; document ON as explicit opt-in. Also: CURL_CA_BUNDLE=auto + CURL_CA_FALLBACK=OFF -> silent HTTPS failure if system CA is missing. Recommend CURL_CA_FALLBACK=ON. 3. GIT-INFO.md -- no version pinning (important) No minimum versions for autotools / OpenSSL; no make check step; no CI sync check with docs/DEPENDENCIES.md. Proposed fix: state min versions (autoconf >= 2.69, automake >= 1.16, libtool >= 2.4, OpenSSL >= 3.0.0) + add make check + CI link-linter. Why it matters TLS client = trust anchor for billions of connections. Supply-chain attacks (XZ Utils 2024, event-stream 2018) prove this is not theoretical. OpenSSF Gold requires source verification and reproducible builds. Related Vishap audits: sess-2026-10-16-111023-03 (INSTALL), sess-2026-10-16-111023-04 (INSTALL-CMAKE), sess-2026-10-16-090837-02 (GIT-INFO). In our case it is the GTK3 vfunc of nested widgets performing recursive , plus a matplotlib canvas drawn from the same path, producing several nested C->Py->C round-trips. This is **not** a generic "every GTK + Python app" issue: most GTK3 apps have a simple (or no) , and GTK4 apps don't use at all, so the required re-entrancy depth is rarely reached. Pitivi happens to trigger it, which is why it is reproducible here. The ASan trace above is a real, reproducible case; a small standalone reproducer would require GTK + nested custom-drawn widgets + a Python vfunc, and is worth having.

text: Let's take the callback. That one has to call which might return a FATAL. Which then needs to return NGHTTP2_ERR_CALLBACK_FAILURE, as returning 0 would make nghttp2 unaware that the session now is in a fatal situation. This makes return this error. Which we check in our ingress processing and return a CURLE_RECV_ERROR. Ingress process is called in 3 locations. Which then, in this PR, also causes error returns. Normally, we offer tracing of success/errors at the end of such calls. However, when nghttp2 is fatal, we have to skip such tracing as retrieving current session properties like window sizes is no longer safe. These are the main IO parts. Then there are other calls like "is the connection alive", "send a ping", "how many streams can you do in parallel" and "this transfer shuts down now", etc. In total, this PR has now 41 places where it checks for a fatal situation. And we are not sure we caught all of them. Because some functions *may* cause a call to an nghttp2 function, or not, depending on the situation. But assume we get this right. Then doing maintenance work in this code is dangerous. You might open new code paths where fatalness appears and is now longer checked properly. Can the whole 3000 lines of implementation be restructured better? Sure. It took about 4 years to come from the existing version to this one which is like 10-20 times more performant and efficient in memory handling. We can start again. Could be fun (and of course, we need a similar solution for ngtcp2/nghttp3 I assume now). But what do we do in the meantime? So, for practical purposes, we need to place a layer on top of the nghttp2/3/ngtcp2 APIs which tracks the fatal-ness and denies calls in such a situation. I see no other way forward.

text: A "good" hash implementation is one that is unlikely to hash two keys that are different to the same value. It follows that data that appears different to humans, and is systematically different to computers (especially when it is different regardless of underlying OS proclivities regarding the exact separator character), should generally not hash equal. @user is completely correct (and there is a sort of inevitability from hashing things) that this does not have to be true at all points, but we would probably like it to not be false for no reason. We do not have to invest an enormous amount of thought here (or invoke elements of the discussion I would encourage us to avoid) to justify "a hit in speed is worth this improvement in quality". Hopefully it does not make anything ten times slower. Even two times slower would be surprising, really. Simply test some options, find out, and maybe come back to discuss if it is somehow magically ten times slower (or whatever else seems terrifyingly too big) and otherwise we can probably just let a reviewer make a judgement call.

text: Following up with a concrete proposal. It builds on nojnhuh's DRA framing above, kannon92's point that a dedicated driver is too much for this case, and the JobSet migration path jianqiaol and tenzen-y described in kubernetes-sigs/jobset#1363. **Summary:** add an opt-in exclusivity setting to , enforced natively by the TAS placement algorithm, so JobSet, LWS and DisaggregatedSet stop implementing it separately. No DRA driver is needed. I would write it as a separate KEP building on KEP-5732, since its Future Extensions section says follow-up features go in separate KEPs. ### API The scope enum answers the scope question for alpha and leaves room for a value later without a new field. The gate name is a placeholder. ### Semantics For a PodGroup G with on key K: 1. Placement generation skips any domain of K that holds scheduled or assumed pods of another PodGroup in G's namespace with on K. Counting assumed pods covers the race JobSet had to handle (kubernetes-sigs/jobset#341). 2. Once G has pods in a domain, other such groups skip that domain. Exclusivity is symmetric and opt-in: groups that do not set are not affected, as with the controllers' anti-affinity today. Keeping all other pods out remains a taint concern. 3. The whole group is checked against a domain before the domain is chosen, so no leader commits to a domain the rest of the group cannot fit in. This comes from KEP-5732 Phase 2 unchanged. 4. It is checked at scheduling time only, like , and is immutable like the rest of . ### Out of scope for alpha - scope. JobSet keeps its annotation for cross-namespace exclusivity until this exists. - CompositePodGroups. is shared with , so validation rejects there in alpha. DisaggregatedSet slices are the main reason to add it next. - Priority. JobSet limits exclusivity to one priority level (kubernetes-sigs/jobset#687). Whether workload-aware preemption may evict one exclusive group to give its domain to another is an open question for the KEP. - DRA. The API describes the request, not how domains are published, so a DRA-backed implementation stays possible later, along the lines nojnhuh described above. ### What it unblocks - Exclusivity together with gang scheduling. LWS rejects that combination (KEP-666 rule 10). In JobSet it can deadlock because followers wait behind the leader, so it is being rejected there too (kubernetes-sigs/jobset#1357). - JobSet can replace the annotation with for same-namespace exclusivity, the path described in kubernetes-sigs/jobset#1363. Its exclusive unit is the child Job, which maps to the per-Job leaf PodGroups discussed in kubernetes-sigs/jobset#1365. - LWS is graduating the annotation to as a standalone field, mutually exclusive with WAS for now (kubernetes-sigs/lws#1064). With this constraint, LWS can translate that field into its PodGroups instead of rejecting the combination. - Kueue gets one constraint in WAS terms instead of a per-controller annotation, once TAS placement is delegated to WAS (kubernetes-sigs/kueue#13151). That addresses kubernetes-sigs/kueue#15057. Kueue TAS has no exclusive mode today, so defining it in WAS first also avoids a Kueue-only version that the in-tree scheduler would later have to match. - It fits the sibling placement optimization in kubernetes/kubernetes#142726: for exclusive siblings, the only placement that changes between children is the domain the previous child took. @user, as the KEP-5732 author, does this direction work for you as a follow-up KEP? If so, I will open it in kubernetes/enhancements and prototype the placement filter, with scalability numbers against the affinity approach. This would target the cycle after 1.38, so it does not compete with the work already in flight.

text:
Still present on 2026.10.1 (core, Supervisor 2026.10.2), 10 AiDot bulbs, US account.

The refresh call fails with a 400 and error code 21025:

ERROR (MainThread) [aidot.client] async_refresh_token ClientError: 400, message='',
url='http {'code': 21025, 'desc': 'Please login again.'}
 File "/usr/local/lib/python3.14/site-packages/aidot/client.py", line 201, in async_refresh_token
 File "/usr/local/lib/python3.14/site-packages/aidot/client.py", line 212, in async_refresh_token

followed by a 401 on the houses endpoint:

ERROR (MainThread) [aidot.client] async_get ClientError: 401, message='',
url='http {'code': 21026, 'desc': 'Please login again.'}

and then the local device clients fail their handshake, which is what the user actually sees:

ERROR (MainThread) [aidot.device_client] <device_id>:read status error 0 bytes read on a total of 8 expected bytes

Why the entry never recovers

async_auto_login in coordinator.py only performs a full login when there is no access token stored:

if self.client.login_info.get(CONF_ACCESS_TOKEN) is None:
 await self.client.async_post_login()

Once a stale access token has been persisted to the config entry, the integration is in a refresh-only state forever. The refresh 400s, nothing clears the dead token, and no code path ever falls back to async_post_login(). That matches what we see in practice:

action | result -- | -- delete and re-add the integration | works — no token, so it does a full login reload the config entry | works temporarily leave it alone | bulbs go unavailable one by one as cached credentials age out

No reauth flow is offered to the user. AidotAuthFailed is translated to ConfigEntryAuthFailed during updates, but the refresh failure above does not appear to surface as that exception, so the entry stays loaded with dead credentials rather than prompting for re-authentication.

Impact

Bulbs drop individually, not all at once, so it reads as flaky hardware rather than an auth problem. In our case one bulb logged 82 errors in a day against 9 for each of its nine siblings, all at -40 dBm with perfect Wi-Fi uptime — which sent us chasing a hardware fault that did not exist. The vendor app keeps working throughout, because it uses the cloud path rather than the local one.

Suggested fix

Fall back to a full async_post_login() when the refresh fails, rather than only when the token is absent — or clear the stored access token on a 400/401 from refreshToken so the existing "no token" branch takes over on the next update.

Happy to test a patch.

text: Just an update: recently started working on integrating mimalloc v3 in CPython (sorry, I hope this does not interfere with your work @user -- I wasn't aware this effort was started). I am hoping mimalloc v3 can become a "drop-in" without needing any patches from the CPython side -- so we can easily upgrade mimalloc in the future if there are security fixes or new features (like the recent profiler hooks) etc. The main item that I added is a good interface for the quiescent-state-based-reclamation (QSBR), and I think I found a good abstraction for this where all lifetime management is now done on the mimalloc side (and part of the regular release). Hope this design can work as the interface is now more general and abstract (so maybe it can work for other runtimes as well). With the new first-class heaps in mimalloc v3, we can make heaps that are QSBR enabled and for those the pages are tracked so we never free the memory if there might still be outstanding readers. The CPython side only needs to define helpers for the actual QSBR goals etc. This is quite minimal now (<http I implemented all this on the mimalloc side where this gets enabled by defining . Now, I don't know CPython very well, so I used an agent to interface CPython with the new v3 API and created a fork here: <http (this is temporary and more a proof of concept and to help others/Sam to integrate this; I can make it into a PR if that is better?) The actual changes to CPython are in [commit e253ecc2](http while the other commits are just including the new vendored mimalloc v3 sources. *It all seems to work already* :-) -- but again, I am not an expert here so someone needs to review the changes and see if it indeed is all ok; @user: hope you can take a look? Here are some other more minor parts that were addressed as summarized by an agent: ## CPython-side changes in my fork The following are in [commit e253ecc2](http in the cpython fork. - [x] Heaps per interpreter instead of tags. Create 4 per interpreter (mem, object, gc, gc_pre). Each thread state gets its per-thread heaps once with and allocates through . Pages never leave their heap and reclaim only happens within a heap. So , the per-interpreter abandoned pools and / all go away. Subprocs aren't needed, and wouldn't fit: one OS thread can run thread states from several interpreters, but can only belong to one subproc. - [x] Simpler GC walk. It becomes per interpreter, covering all threads and abandoned pages. No loop over thread states, no lock, no separate abandoned visit. - [x] Smaller installed headers. then only needs opaque pointers, so only has to be installed. - [x] Cache the per-thread theaps in the thread state. has a single cache slot, so switching between 4 heaps would keep hitting the slow lookup. Get a with in each thread state and use . (or if the size is statically known). - [x] Already upstream in v3: the macro, the configurable debug fill bytes, , the UWP fix and the microsoft/mimalloc#1321 CodeQL fixes. The gh-123022 patch no longer applies. ## Mimalloc v3 changes These are already committed in the latest in mimalloc. - [x] Per-heap debug-fill offset. v3 fills whole blocks on alloc and free. Py_DEBUG free-threaded builds need the object header bytes left intact. Fixed in commit fc238b62. - [x] Public "page owner thread id" call. needs it. Abandoned pages in v3 report 0 or 4, so it should return 0 for both. CPython would replace the segment lookup with: . Added in commit 9dac1fec. - [x] Explicit "abandon this thread's per-heap state" call. The internal version, , is commented out. CPython needs one on the owning thread (thread state cleared while the OS thread lives on), and one usable from another thread when the owner is dead ( of other threads, ). Add and (commit 318f6817). Not sure in-how-far this is still needed with first-class heaps and heap-destroy/delete. Hope we can avoid calling this. - [x] Fork safety. v2 was nearly lock-free. v3 uses some pthread mutexes and has no fork handlers, so a fork can deadlock the child. In the child, dead threads' pages also stay "owned", and a new thread can reuse the same thread id. Suggest or . Fixed in commit 1b7e73f3, 7ea8bfc0, and c084f15a. - [x] Heap-walk bug (reproduced). text: I have opened #33237 with a fix and regression tests. I also want to make the single thread case more explicit, because it doesn't depend on another thread calling into OpenSSL. Suppose a listener L, created with the default flags, has two accepted connections, S0 and S1. A call polling [L, S0] registers L first. While translating S0, it can demultiplex an ordinary datagram for S1 and signal the listener. Cleanup then waits for another registration held by the same call, leaving it stuck waiting on itself. The reproducer makes this sequence deterministic using to leave the datagram pending during the initial readiness check. Once enters the blocking path, it ignores that flag and processes the datagram. The flag doesn't provide a workaround. The requested timeout doesn't bound the wait in cleanup, so a timeout of one second can still leave the call stuck indefinitely. The PR includes regression tests that exercise this sequence with a real datagram. Those cases pass with the fix and hit their watchdog with the old code. @user Since this can hang an ordinary server loop with just one thread using DTLS, I think the fix should land before 4.1 release.

text: Your instinct likely exists because is secure (but maybe not performant) to substitute a cryptographically secure hash algorithm where a weaker hash would also be secure. Cryptographic hashes often remain secure for some purposes, even if you do things that would break cryptographic security, like repeating nonces. In this case, it's the way data is fed to the hash that seems to be the core issue, rather than the hash algorithm. This is a known issue in hashing implementations, where parts of the data are skipped or combined, leading to the same raw data being provided to the hash for different inputs. To answer the question at the top of the ticket: - the threat model for HashDoS requires that attackers can't predictably cause collisions, as long as the hash table seed is random - if we allow some and to collide ~~by default~~, this creates predictable attacker-controlled collisions for paths in hash tables (edit: for many applications using Rust) - the performance cost of including path separators as characters is likely low This is a separate question to other hash improvements (like a length prefix per part, which is not required for the HashDoS threat model) or changing the hash output width or algorithm. These are much larger changes, possibly with large performance impacts.

text: Thanks for checking the raw response, that settles it. iCloud already leaves the moved occurrence out of its response for the narrow range, so this is a server-side issue. RFC 4791 (section 9.9) requires a time-range filter to match against every instance of a recurring event, including moved ones with their new start. iCloud apparently ignore the moved occurrence's new date when matching the time range, and only returns the event once the range includes its original date. Working around this in HA by default would mean querying much wider ranges for every CalDAV server, and even that wouldn't be reliable, since an occurrence can be moved arbitrarily far. The right place for a fix is python-caldav, the library the integration uses. It has per-server compatibility profiles with workarounds, and since caldav 3.5.0 (which Home Assistant will use from 2026.11) there's even a dedicated iCloud profile. text: I got a little nerdsniped this weekend and spent a decent chunk of time thinking about this. I ended up landing on a workaround I'm happy enough with that I opened http The solution I ended up with is to define an iterator type in PyO3 that defines . When CPython builds a list from the iterator, it takes a single outer critical section on the list, bypassing the overhead of repeatedly entering a critical section on the list for each list item. It relies on smuggling a pointer into via a thread local without incurring interpreter overhead to get it from the type data for the iterator type. It's possible to use type data but it ends up being slower. It doesn't help for small lists but it helps a lot for large lists, so I also had to introduce a threshold list size to start using this optimization. I also experimented with @user's "built a tuple then convert via " idea. That performs decently on x86_64 for objects that already exist and for moderately sized lists, but it performs poorly or is a wash otherwise. Because atomics are cheaper on aarch64, it always ends up being a wash or even marginally slower on ARM. Taking an outer critical section also performs decently on x86_64 and is a wash or an outright loser on aarch64. This is all summarized in this plot:

text: Follow-up after f52a2ad and 927cf77. Findings 1, 3, 5 and 8 from the review above are resolved by those commits, thanks. The remaining point is the shape of the "keep the service cause" rule, and a proposal for where the needed information should come from. **Trade-off of the current 5 s window** f52a2ad treats every incoming telegram within of a service call as feedback. That also swallows a genuine wall-switch press or a stop pressed mid-travel in that window: the state changes with the automation's context and no sender event fires. For covers, the window is also too short: the final position feedback after a 20 s travel is attributed to the actuator and displaces the automation cause. **Proposal: classify telegrams by command vs. state address** - A telegram to a *command* address ( , , , ...) is a new actor. Attribute it to the sender, even inside the window. - A telegram to a *state* address ( , , , ...) is a report. While an HA action is in progress, keep the entity's current cause and fire no sender event. Otherwise attribute it to the actuator as now. That keeps autonomous actuator logic (sun shading, internal scenes) attributed to the actuator, which is the correct actor in that case. - "In progress" means the existing 5 s service window for lights and switches. For covers use plus a grace of about a second after the last callback that saw it traveling, instead of any arithmetic. This also works for a bus-initiated travel: the final feedback keeps the wall switch's cause instead of replacing it with the actuator. - Echo on the command address (no separate state address configured): inside the window, a write to the command address carrying the value HA just sent is a confirmation and keeps the service cause; a different value is a real actor. **Where to define command vs. state** This belongs in xknx. already matches the destination against , and the passive list, so recording which side matched is a small addition, and is new in 4.0.0 so a field like can be added without breaking anyone. Two details to settle there: the passive addresses of both sides are merged in , so the side has to be recorded at init or the lists kept apart; and a GA used as both command and state should classify as command. The flag should only say what the telegram is; whether to attribute stays an HA decision. I'd release that as xknx 4.1 and bump it here. If release timing is a problem, HA can bridge the gap by collecting the yaml keys and the UI selector's field into a set at entity construction, to be removed once the xknx field exists. **Documentation note** Activity only logs changes of the state string. A sun-shading move from open to 30 % keeps the cover "open", and a light dimmed by its actuator stays "on", so neither produces a row regardless of attribution. text: We investigated how the ARC8 ( ) firmware handles the 6-digit PIN and local authentication (tracked in allenporter/pyrainbird#632) and found a couple of behaviors that explain the and 15-minute lockout you are seeing: 1. **How the 15-minute brute-force lockout works:** - After 5 failed authentication attempts, the ARC8 locks out local HTTP requests for **15 minutes (900 seconds)**. During those 15 minutes, **every** request returns —even if you enter the **correct** password. - Additionally, the failed-attempt counter stays at in RAM after the 15-minute cooldown expires (only a reboot resets it to ). That means after waiting 15 minutes, you only get **1 attempt** before a wrong password immediately locks it out for another 15 minutes. - **Tip:** **Unplug / power-cycle your ARC8 controller** before testing again so the failed-attempt counter resets to and any active 15-minute lockout is cleared immediately. 2. **Why the 6-digit PIN in the Rain Bird 2.0 app may not match the local password:** - The Rain Bird 2.0 app connects to the ARC8 over Bluetooth (BLE) and the Rain Bird Cloud (neither of which uses the local password after setup). - When setting or changing the 6-digit PIN over Bluetooth in the app, the ARC8 firmware only saves that PIN to local flash storage when the **Wi-Fi setup step** completes in the same Bluetooth session. If Bluetooth briefly reconnected during initial setup, or if the PIN was changed later over Bluetooth without re-saving Wi-Fi settings, the local password stored on the controller may still be its previous PIN (or blank). - **Tip:** If your current 6-digit PIN still fails immediately after power-cycling the ARC8, go into the **Rain Bird 2.0 app -> Settings -> Reset Wi-Fi / Reconfigure Wi-Fi** (while near the controller on Bluetooth) so it walks through the PIN + Wi-Fi join flow in a single session and commits the 6-digit PIN to flash, then power-cycle the ARC8 once and try adding it in Home Assistant using that 6-digit PIN.

It does not send a command while waiting for , and it sends the tagged completion for IDLE only after . The late completes the earlier SEARCH. The client timeout does not cancel that server-side command, and leaves its tag pending. On unmodified main, the delayed completion triggers the in . RFC 3501 section 2.2.1 describes this response ordering explicitly: Section 5.5 permits multiple commands to be in progress when there is no ambiguity. SEARCH does not affect IDLE, and their distinct tags identify the two completions. Here, the earlier SEARCH completion is received while the IDLE continuation is pending; both command lines have already been sent. RFC 2177 requires the tagged completion for IDLE after ; this exchange does that, while the other tag belongs to SEARCH. Other clients also account for tagged or unexpected responses during IDLE. [Thunderbird's IMAP parser](http has a dedicated branch: it processes the expected IDLE tag normally, and turns a different tag into a controlled fatal error and server alert. [Angus Mail's ](http dispatches each response and ends IDLE only when the tag matches the IDLE command. Python clients show both defensive approaches. [imapclient's ](http passes each received line to an untagged-response parser; a tagged line fails its protocol check and raises the library's ([check](http [aioimaplib](http routes tagged lines to its [pending-command handler](http which raises the library's exception for an unexpected tag.

text: In cmd/go/internal/doc/dirs.go, findCodeRoots calls vendorEnabled, which calls getMainModuleAnd114. That function runs go list -m -f <format> and assumes the output describes exactly one main module. In workspace mode, go list -m prints every workspace module, so the code picks lines[0..3], which belong to the first workspace module (example.com/a). That module has a vendor/ directory and go >= 1.14, so vendorEnabled returns true. The search roots then become GOROOT plus a/vendor and a. The go list -m all branch, which would add the dependency module roots, is never reached, so the suffix lookup in matchingPackages cannot find any dependency. strace confirms that only go list -m and go env GOFLAGS are executed. An explicit -mod in GOFLAGS skips the automatic vendor detection, which is why GOFLAGS=-mod=readonly works around the problem. GOWORK=off also works around it. Possible fix: when a go.work file is in effect, don't infer vendor mode from a single module's vendor/. In workspace mode, vendoring is controlled by the vendor/ next to go.work. Alternatively, get the main module(s) and vendor mode from the in-process modload state, since parseArgs already initialises it, instead of shelling out to go list -m. Related but distinct: #76248 and #41501 (suffix lookup vs. package name / /vN). ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── Notes: - The fix suggestion and the claim that the workspace-level vendor/ is what counts come from my reading of the code. I didn't verify them against the docs. - I added the ai: title suffix because of your org rule. Drop it if golang/go conventions take priority. - Nothing has been filed. text: Some data from Korean (Hangul), as of 1.99: **Modern Korean is fine today**, in both NFC and NFD: and both print unescaped. **NFD Hangul is not rare in practice.** File names created on macOS are commonly stored as conjoining jamo (NFD), and the resulting "jamo split" (자소 분리) is a well-known everyday annoyance for Korean users exchanging files between macOS and Windows. So output, zip entries etc. regularly contain NFD Hangul. Any rule based on (as in #158286) would escape every medial vowel and final consonant (U+1161–1175, U+11A8–11C2), turning into , i.e. nearly every other character. Please keep conjoining jamo printable. **Hangul fillers should stay escaped.** U+115F, U+1160, U+3164 and U+FFA0 are default-ignorable and render invisibly; U+3164 in particular is widely abused for "blank" user names and spoofing. Escaping them matches the "surprising/invisible characters should be visible" goal. **Tone marks (U+302E, U+302F)** are grapheme extenders and are currently escaped ( ). They are spacing marks (gc=Mc), visibly rendered next to the syllable, much like U+FF9E/U+FF9F which are already exempted (#158057). They mostly appear in Middle Korean text, so this is lower priority, but a principle like "don't escape visible spacing marks" would cover them. I've opened #164514, a test-only PR pinning the current Hangul behaviour (jamo printable, fillers escaped), and have a small branch for the tone marks ready if that direction is wanted.

text: I like the new wording of the description: However, unfortunately, I just realized, it actually doesn't always get the sign right :-( Consider det([[1e-300,0],[0,1e-300]]). Your function will return 0.0, which is the true answer correctly rounded to nearest float, so it's definitely correct, and it satisfies the <=1.5ulps contract. But, for the purposes of exact sidedness testing predicates, the sign of that isn't right: the mathematically exact true answer is positive, so the true sign is +1, not 0. So it would be wrong to say that it gets the sign right. It would still be nice to say something here, but I'm not sure exactly what can be said that would be correct. Another option (which I'm not seriously suggesting) would be to detect this case (if that's even feasible) and return (plus or minus) the smallest positive float, instead of 0. The <=1.5ulps contract would still be satisfied, and the "always gets the sign right" would then be satisfied as well. If I remember correctly, [google's s2 library](http actually does this somewhere, in the spirit of taking robust sidedness testing really really seriously. But I wouldn't suggest trying to play such games in this PR.

text: Follow-up with raw data from my gateway (firmware 8.3.5433, pyenphase 4.0.6), plus a working workaround for anyone affected. ## Confirmation: the gateway itself reports wrong values From the config-entry diagnostics, returns: | eim meter | whLifetime | whToday | whLastSevenDays | |---|---|---|---| | production | 32712449.204 | 32712449.204 | 32712449.204 | | total-consumption | 31479621.431 | 31479621.431 | 31479621.431 | | net-consumption | -1232827.773 | 0 | 0 | So the Envoy reports its lifetime totals in the "today" and "last seven days" fields, and the integration passes them through unchanged. That matches the earlier comments that this is a firmware change rather than an integration bug. I also checked the daily values derived from the lifetime sensors against Enlighten (Enphase cloud) for 12-18 Oct: production 228.8 kWh (HA) vs 228.3 kWh (Enlighten), consumption 237.6 vs 237.5 kWh, with a matching day-by-day shape. So the **lifetime sensors are reliable**, and Enphase's cloud calculates correct daily figures. Only the gateway's own "today" / "last seven days" fields are wrong. ## Workaround: daily meters from the lifetime sensors Settings > Devices & services > Helpers > Create helper > **Utility Meter**. Create one per sensor: 1. Name: e.g. . Input sensor: **Lifetime energy production** (not "net"). Meter reset cycle: **Daily**. 2. Name: e.g. . Input sensor: **Lifetime energy consumption** (not "net"). Meter reset cycle: **Daily**. For both, set these options: - **Periodically resetting: off.** With it on, any drop in the lifetime counter (for example the known step-downs when an inverter counter overflows) is treated as a reset and the full lifetime value gets added to the day. - **Sensor always available: on.** The Envoy sensors go briefly overnight and during dropouts, and this keeps the meter from showing unknown. - Leave Net consumption and Delta values off. The lifetime sensors are in MWh, so the new meters are too. After creating each one, open its settings (gear icon) and change **Unit of measurement** to **kWh** for a readable value. Each meter starts counting from the moment it is created, so the first day is partial. From the first midnight on, the values are full-day totals. Optional, a daily net value (negative when exporting, matching the integration's net consumption sign): a template sensor helper with this state template, unit kWh, device class Energy, state class Total: Replace the two entity IDs with your new meters' IDs. text: Pay close attention to the second sentence that you quoted. That paragraph is saying that the server can send a tagged completion response from some other command after receiving from the client, but BEFORE it sends back to the client. That is, while the command continuation request **is still pending**. This is more clear if you understand the protocol as a whole, rather than taking the paragraph above out of context. When the server sends a command continuation request response (which starts with ), it is in the middle of receiving a multi-line command from the client, indicating that it's ready to receive the next part. It would not make sense for it to send unrelated data (like tagged responses to an earlier command) in that state. Consider also that the IDLE command (which is not the only command that triggers continuation requests from the server) corroborates this in [RFC 2177](http Note that tagged responses are not listed among the things the server can send during IDLE. (And in case you missed it, the IDLE command is active as soon as the server sends its continuation request, which starts with ) So, I do not see a bug in imaplib here. This is why I asked you what server behaves as you describe. Ah, I see. I suggest you contact the author of that application, and let them know that they have a bug in their IMAP service.

text: I hit this and eventually found this old issue. Reproduced with Go 1.27.2 and go1.28-devel_dfc6f7db9b on darwin/arm64. The aliasing happens inside the fuzz mutator, before the target runs. Demonstration without modifying either argument: Fails immediately: The seeds were "first" and "second". Here, b contains a's mutated bytes followed by "ond", the leftover tail of "second". Replaying the saved input passes: Looks like [mutator.mutate](http copies every value it mutates into one shared buffer, , and stores that slice as the new value. If two mutated arguments share the same chain, they share the buffer, and later mutation overwrites the earlier argument. This also explains both the failure in the original report and why replay passes: the corpus file records the overwritten contents, but replay decodes each value into a separate slice. Some relevant history of the fuzzer: - [CL 324849](http introduced the shared buffer - [#48308](http found that strings changed after the fuzz function returned - [CL 351312](http fixed that by copying strings - An earlier version of that fix also copied values ([CL 349989, patch set 1](http but that was [dropped in review](http to avoid an alloc per exec. The documentation says not to retain arguments between executions. So this behaviour doesn't sound like it's by design. The aliasing is between arguments of the same call. I've been preparing a change that gives each argument its own reusable scratch buffer - while still complying with the max budget.

text: Thanks for the reproducer, confirmed. On a 30-bit PGO+LTO build with , all three cases go wrong on this PR ( , and instead of the -based results), and they are correct on the merge base and on non-JIT builds. The root cause is what you described: can now return a non-compact int, but the optimizer still models its result as a unique compact int. The guard on the following int op gets removed, and that op is rewritten to its variant, which reads from a 2-digit value. Folding the guards into the op also cost the guard elimination and added , as you pointed out, so I don't think this approach is salvageable as is. Also, apologies for the confusion in my earlier reply: I said I'd narrowed this to the int64 path, but what's pushed is the shrink-subtract specialization. Please ignore that comment. I'm reworking it along the lines you suggested: leave the compact specializations exactly as they are on main, and handle the multi-digit case separately. The simplest version I have uses . When the operands aren't both compact, / (and the in-place forms) get a descriptor whose guard is a plain exact- type check and whose action calls / directly, skipping the dispatch. The result is typed as but not as compact, so any later compact-int ops keep their guards. and the optimizer are untouched, it doesn't depend on , and it covers addition too. Your reproducer passes with it, and I've added it as a regression test in . Numbers: wall-clock microbenchmarks on a cloud VM (isolated cores, ) turned out too noisy for a change this small. PGO layout alone moved untouched compact ops by ±5–8%, and repeated runs of the same LTO-only binary drifted by up to ~9%. So I measured user-space instructions per op instead ( , difference between 3M and 1M iterations, empty loop subtracted, 5 repeats each), on 30-bit builds of the merge base : | instructions/op | sub compact | add compact | sub 2-digit shrink | sub 3-digit shrink | sub wide | add wide | |---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:| | base (LTO) | 126 | 127 | 256 | 365 | 348 | 347 | | rework (LTO) | 128 | 127 | 221 | 330 | 313 | 315 | | base (PGO+LTO) | 126 | 125 | 216 | 323 | 304 | 291 | | this PR (PGO+LTO) | 125 | 125 | 186 | 369 | 305 | 294 | | rework (PGO+LTO) | 127 | 127 | 182 | 291 | 270 | 258 | | base (PGO+LTO, JIT) | 113 | 114 | 241 | 350 | 330 | 319 | | this PR (PGO+LTO, JIT) | 116 | 113 | 198 | 348 | 331 | 317 | | rework (PGO+LTO, JIT) | 113 | 112 | 215 | 292 | 272 | 261 | So on this base the rework saves 26–58 instructions per wide add/sub, and compact ops are unchanged within noise. Rebased on current main (7dbc7975db), it saves 30–39 instructions per wide add/sub (~10–12%) in all three configurations, JIT included, again with compact ops unchanged. This PR only helps the 2-digit shrinking case and is 46 instructions worse on 3-digit shrinking without the JIT, which is another reason to drop it. On pyperformance (LTO-only builds, no PGO, one run each, pinned to an isolated core) there's no measurable change. The geometric mean comes out at 1.03x faster, but benchmarks with no wide-int arithmetic moved ±10–20% in both directions (e.g. 1.20x faster, 1.14x slower), so I read that as noise. That's expected, since very little of the suite does non-compact int add/sub. The earlier PGO+LTO runs were worse: this PR and the rework both came out within 0–3% of base on the geometric mean, with similar swings. and fail on 3.16 for every build. I'll open the rework as a new PR and close this one, since the approach is different enough.

text: One trade-off worth flagging. Because the guard here is a pure type check, compact ints pass it too. A site that happens to specialize while it sees a wide value therefore stays on for compact values as well, and never goes back to / . On main, such a site fails to specialize, and on a later attempt it picks up the compact form. I also built the alternative: a guard function that only accepts exact ints that are *not both compact*, so compact pairs deopt and respecialize. Instructions per op ( , same method as in the description, 30-bit builds of 7dbc7975db): **Extra cost per compact op at a site that was specialized on a wide value:** | | main | this PR (type-only guard) | guard function | |---|---:|---:|---:| | LTO | 0 | +34 | +1 | | PGO+LTO | +1 | +19 | +1 | | PGO+LTO, JIT | +63 | +36 | +87 | **Instructions saved per wide add/sub ( ), compared with main:** | | this PR | guard function | |---|---:|---:| | LTO | 38–39 | 21–22 | | PGO+LTO | 30–31 | 11–13 | | PGO+LTO, JIT | 31–33 | 11–15 | The guard function fixes the pinning without the JIT, but it cuts the gain on wide ints by half or more: calling the guard through the pointer and checking compactness costs more. Under the JIT it is worse than both main and this PR in the pinned case, most likely because each compact pair fails the guard inside the trace and exits it (I haven't confirmed that with the JIT's stats). It also stops the optimizer from dropping the guard when the operand types are known. So I've kept the type-only guard. The pinning only affects sites that specialize while seeing a wide value and later see mostly compact ones, and the cost there is bounded. If you'd rather never be slower than main in the default build, the guard-function version is ready and I can switch to it.

text: I gave the issue to Claude Code and told it to spin-up a subagent for the ASM/IR debugging, here's the transcript: ## What goes wrong - The bad code is in fdeflate's Decompressor::read. In src/decompress.rs:160, fill_buffer advances input by (63 - self.nbits) / 8 bytes. - The overflow check makes that subtraction nuw in LLVM IR. The IR is correct. - On AArch64, an 8-bit value in a 32-bit register can have junk in the upper bits. Here they hold the other fields of the Huffman table entry. - LLVM 22 masks the result with and #0xff before shifting it, and LLVM 23 drops that mask. It trusts the nuw flag, but the flag stopped being valid once the subtraction was widened to 32 bits. - The junk bits then get shifted into the byte count, so input skips the wrong number of bytes. That corrupts the PNG data. Without overflow checks, that code path has no nuw, so the bug doesn't trigger. ## Why only this setup fails The subagent says the final thin-LTO code generation for the doctest binary runs at opt-level 0. On AArch64, that means GlobalISel instead of the usual instruction selector. Its evidence: - The shipped assembly looks like -O0 output. - LLVM 23's llc -O0 reproduces it byte for byte. I couldn't confirm the opt-level from the logged rustc arguments, because rustdoc passes most flags through a response file the wrapper script didn't save. This is my guess, not a test result: it would explain why only thin LTO fails, and why release builds, which code-generate at opt-level 3, probably aren't affected. ## Reproducer Run with llc -O0. LLVM 22.1.8 emits and w8, w8, #0xff after subs, and LLVM 23.1.0 doesn't: target triple = "arm64-apple-macosx11.0.0" define i64 @user(i8 %n) { %r = sub nuw nsw i8 63, %n %s = lshr i8 %r, 3 %z = zext nneg i8 %s to i64 ret i64 %z } The subagent's guess at the cause is a change from LLVM 22 to 23 in how GlobalISel's legalizer folds zero-extensions and truncations. It didn't bisect LLVM to confirm this. ## Other findings - The same missing mask appears at about 20 similar sites in read. Most get a clean byte input, so only some of them corrupt anything. - The compressor functions and build_table have no harmful differences. So the bug is on the PNG reading side, not the writing side. I'll prepare the reproducer for LLVM. Maybe we should close this issue.

text: Pushed 586441c, rebased onto current first (no conflicts). It addresses the two newest review points, both of which were right. **Renewal now runs on a timer.** My earlier change only refreshed the session when a client asked for its WebRTC configuration. That callback is synchronous, so it can't wait for a new session: after the camera sat idle past expiry, the first browser got no TURN servers for that attempt even though the refresh succeeded straight afterwards. The session is now renewed five minutes before its reported expiry, scheduled whenever one is stored (from a refresh or from an offer), and cancelled when the entity is removed. A fetch still in flight at removal can't re-arm it. **Failed fetches are retried.** If the startup fetch, or an expired session's replacement, failed, nothing tried again until an offer happened to repopulate the cache. A failed fetch is now retried after five minutes, and a configuration request that finds the cache empty or expired starts a refresh straight away rather than waiting for the timer. Two edge cases I chose deliberately: a session with no reported expiry gets no timer, since there is nothing to renew ahead of (otherwise it would refresh every minute indefinitely), and renewals are never closer together than a minute. Tests cover renewal firing on schedule with no configuration request, a failed fetch being retried, an empty cache refetching on request, the no-expiry case, and the timer stopping on removal. I also broke each behaviour on purpose to confirm the matching test fails. Two older tests had a relay mock returning a bare from ; it now returns a , as the library does. 112 tests in pass locally, mypy reports nothing for the integration, and hassfest and ruff are clean.

text: Hmm, i've had another thought. I mentioned a while ago that we could amortize the type storage by storing them top-level for all tests in a single file. Not only would this share types between multiple tests, but we could also share types between targets (e.g. most s are identical, target-to-target). The difficulty with that is knowing when types in that file should be deleted. Since they're only "observed" on a test-by-test basis, we wouldnt be able to tell whether types are unused because it's no longer needed vs when it's unused because it's only used in a different test. That can be solved by tagging the types with the tests they're used in. We can check against that to ensure that we've used every type a given test expects, and when blessing, we can remove the given tests listing from all types, and then re-add it to each type used in the test. The other issue is conflicting types with the same name. For user defined types in each test, we csn ensure they're namespaced uniquely by adding a compiler option to match the object name to the test name. The tricky part is handling types that differ by OS (e.g. , which uses a on non-windows and a on windows). Additionally, iirc, sum-type enums also arent guaranteed to (and currently dont) choose the same discriminant value on vs for types like that niche optimize on . That's only really a problem if we use a direct mapping though. Instead, we could use a flat array and lookup by index, something like: That would also neatly solve the first issue, since we can just check that every index in is present, and cull any type entry that dont appear in any .
